passages.t: ‘A prayer of one who is afflicted’: ‘But You remain the same’
passages.happening:
The heading does not name an author. It names a kind of person: “A prayer of one who is afflicted, when he grows faint and pours out his lament before the LORD” (verse 1).

The sufferer describes himself in sharp pictures. “For my days vanish like smoke, and my bones burn like glowing embers” (verse 3). “I even forget to eat my bread” (verse 4). “I lie awake; I am like a lone bird on a housetop” (verse 7). He has eaten ashes and mixed his drink with tears (verse 9). “I wither away like grass” (verse 11).

Then the psalm turns from his short days to God. “But You, O LORD, sit enthroned forever” (verse 12). He looks to God to have pity on Zion, which lies in ruins (verses 13 to 16). God “will not despise their prayer” (verse 17). “Let this be written for the generation to come” (verse 18).

At the end he comes back to his own life. “O my God, do not take me in the midst of my days! Your years go on through all generations” (verse 24). The earth and the heavens will wear out like clothing, “But You remain the same, and Your years will never end” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The heading tells the reader what this psalm is for. It is a prayer for anyone who is suffering and has run out of strength. It was kept so that others could pray it.

The pictures come from everyday life. Smoke, embers and grass that dries up in summer show how quickly things vanish. Sitting in ashes was a sign of mourning (Job 2:8). Owls were birds of ruined and empty places. A lone bird on a flat roof is a picture of loneliness anyone could see.

The middle of the psalm speaks of Zion's ‘stones’ and ‘dust’. Most scholars think it comes from the time after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, when the city lay in rubble. One person's suffering and the ruin of the whole city are prayed together.

This is one of the seven psalms the church has called the ‘penitential psalms’, as the note on Psalm 6 explains, though it does not confess a particular sin.
passages.later:
Hebrews quotes verses 25 to 27 and applies them to the Son: “In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands” (Hebrews 1:10). “You will roll them up like a robe; like a garment they will be changed; but You remain the same, and Your years will never end” (Hebrews 1:12).

James writes of “the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (James 1:17). Paul writes, “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).
passages.hard:
Verse 10 says the sufferer feels picked up and thrown aside by God's anger. Does that mean his illness is a punishment? The psalm never names a sin, and the Bible, in Job above all, refuses to say that every illness is a punishment. Many readers take verse 10 as the sufferer's honest account of how it feels, or as tied to the exile of the whole people. If you are ill, this psalm does not mean God is punishing you.

If you are like the man in this psalm, unable to sleep, forgetting to eat, feeling alone like a bird on a roof, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
This psalm was written for you on your worst day. Its heading says so. You may pour out your complaint to God in its words, or in your own.

Then do what the psalm does: look up from your short days to God, who remains the same. The psalm does not say that the suffering ends at once. It says that God does not change, and that he does not despise the prayer of the destitute.
